thread.title: Morning Movers: Texas Instruments Tanks on Earnings; United Continental Sinks

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Morning Movers: Texas Instruments Tanks on Earnings; United Continental Sinks
text:
Stocks are set to open higher this morning after the U.S. touted the benefits of a weaker dollar at Davos and manufacturing surveys continued to show global economic strength .
Illustration: Howard Kingsnorth S&P 500 futures have risen 0.3%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have gained 102 points, or 0.4%. Nasdaq Composite futures have advanced 0.3%. The U.S. dollar has dropped 0.8% against the yen, while the euro has rallied 0.5% versus the dollar. Purchasing manager indexes rose in China , Germany and Japan . The U.S. Markit PMI is scheduled to be released at 9:45 a.m. this morning.
Today should continue what has been a truly amazing run for the market this month. The S&P 500 is up 6.2% so far in January, and has closed at 12 record highs so far this month . And now we're gapping up. That combination—a gain of 6% or more over a three week period, a close at a new high, and a gap up—doesn't happen very often, says Sundial Capital Research's Jason Goepfert. In fact, it's happened just 16 times since 1985, with the last trifecta occurring on March 22, 2000. If you're a short term trader, it's not a great time to be jumping in: Following those occasions, the market was higher one month later just 44% of the time, though the average return of that period was 0%. But if you lengthen your outlook to three months, the market is higher 75% of the time with an average gain of 2.2%.
Amazing. — Ben Levisohn
Morning Movers General Electric (GE) has advanced 0.4% to $16.95 in volatile trading this morning after releasing a disappointing fourth-quarter earnings report and revealing an SEC probe of its recent insurance charge . GE said it earned 27 cents a share on revenue that fell 5% year over year to $31.4 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of 28 cents a share on revenue of $33.93 billion. However, GE reaffirmed that it expects to earn between $1 and $1.07 for the full year, above the $1.01 analysts were expecting. That contrasts with the pessimism ahead of GE's earnings , which isn't surprising given that the stock has performed dismally .
Comcast (CMCSA) is down 2% to $41.56 in early trading, despite reporting a better-than-expected fourth quarter and raising its dividend. Comcast said it earned 49 cents a share, on revenue that rose 4.2% to $21.9 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of 47 cents a share on revenue of $21.8 billion. It also raised its dividend by 21% to 76 cents a share, and said it plans to buy back $5 billion in stock this year. Perhaps investors were hoping for something better from its tax savings .
United Continental (UAL) has tumbled 8% to $77.71 despite its beat-and-raise quarter . United said that it earned $1.40 a share, on revenue that rose 4.3% year over year to $9.44 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of $1.31 a share on $9.41 billion in revenue. For the full year, it said it expects to earn between $6.50 and $8.50 a share, above the $7 analyst estimate. However, investors were spooked by its capacity increases, which it forecast between 4% and 6%. It's a far cry from the cheers United received for its December traffic .
Texas Instruments (TXN) has slumped 7.3% to $111.11 despite its roughly in-line fourth quarter and guidance, hurt by a hit from tax reform . Texas Instruments said it earned $1.09 a share, on revenue that rose 9.8% to $3.75 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of 75 cents a share on $3.74 billion. It forecast earnings between 98 cents and $1.14 a share for the first quarter, on revenue of $3.49 billion to $3.79 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of $1.04 billion a share on revenue of $3.63 billion.
United Technologies (UTX) is off 0.8% at $135 after reporting fourth-quarter earnings about in line with expectations. United Technologies said it earned $1.60 a share on revenue that rose 7% to $15.68 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of $1.56 a share on revenue for $15.34 billion. For the full year, the company expects earnings of $6.85 to $7.10 a share, on revenue of $62.5 billion to $64 billion. Analysts forecast earnings of $6.97 a share on revenue of $62.97 billion.
W.W. Grainger ( GWW) is up 12% to $257 this morning after reporting upbeat fourth-quarter earnings and guidance. Grainger said it earned $2.94 a share on revenue that rose 6.5% year over year to $2.63 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of $2.19 on revenue of $2.57 billion. For the full year, it expects earnings between $12.95 and $14.15, on revenue of $10.74 billion to $11.15 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of $11.41 billion on revenue of $10.88 billion.
— Teresa Rivas
Is the Biotech Rally Just Getting Started? Biotech companies haven't even started reporting earnings yet and already some analysts are trying to tamp down expectations . Technical analysts, however, are starting to get excited about the sector.
Illustration: Getty Images Take Wolfe Research's Rob Ginsberg. He writes that after a roller-coaster ride in recent years, the group has finally broken out to fresh all-time highs, at least on an equal-weight basis, which reinforces his bullish outlook for biotech. Momentum and trends favor equal-weighing over market cap weighting, and small over large, Ginsberg says.
He's not the only one seeing potential in biotech. Fundstrat technical analyst Robert Sluymer says the iShares Nasdaq Biotech ETF (IBB) "remains attractive technically as M&A returns to the sector following a broad 2-year consolidation above support."
We'll find out more when Biogen (BIIB) and Celgene (CELG) get earnings season started for biotech on Thursday morning. — Teresa Rivas
The View From Silicon Valley With so much talk of Apple (AAPL), Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Facebook (FB) putting their corporate tax cut windfalls to use in a frenzy of acquisitions, attention in Silicon Valley has shifted to hot start-ups in emerging markets such as mixed reality and artificial intelligence that could be attractive acquisition targets.
One candidate receiving its share of buzz is VR start-up STRIVR Labs, which has routinely been in the news as a training application . Late Tuesday, it detailed a partnership with U.S. Ski & Snowboard to help Americans medal at next month’s Pyeongchang Winter Olympics in South Korea. For nearly two years, U.S. Olympians’ Lindsey Vonn, Mikaela Shiffrin and others have used 360-degree video and VR to virtually ski race courses at the Olympic venue and at World Cup events.
If results from STRIVR’s other sports training endeavors are any indication, it might give U.S. athletes a sizable edge: The Menlo Park, Calif.-based company claims its VR training results in a 10% improvement in performance and 20% faster reaction times.
The partnership is the latest illustration of how the 3-year-old company has become a staple in training athletes and employees in the NFL, NCAA football, NBA, NHL, Walmart (WMT), United Rentals (URI) and elsewhere. It could be a valuable addition to several large tech companies in pursuit of the multibillion-dollar mixed reality market for training.
“We’re getting a lot of attention from larger companies (as customers). It’s been very fortuitous timing for us,” says Danny Belch, STRIVR’s Chief Strategy Officer. His brother, former Stanford University kicker Derek Belch, is company co-founder.
As for acquisition overtures, Danny Belch is circumspect. “We’re trying to keep our heads down and build great products,” he says. — Jon Swartz
